Cecal Ligation and Puncture (CLP)-induced high-grade sepsis. Eight-week-old male C57Bl/6J mice (Envigo, Gannat, France) were purchased and allowed to acclimate for one week. Mice were randomly assigned to treatment groups and administered either a monoclonal antibody against ACBP/DBI (α-ACBP or aDBI; 4 h and 1 h prior to surgery) or its isotype control, in combination with dexamethasone (DEX) or Phosphate-Buffered Saline (PBS) 1X, administered 1 h before CLP, as previously described 58,59. Sepsis was induced by CLP under isoflurane anesthesia. Briefly, the cecum was exteriorized, ligated at 75% of its length using non-absorbable 4-0 silk suture, and punctured once through-and-through with a 21-gauge needle. A small amount of fecal content was gently extruded, and the cecum was returned to the abdominal cavity. Sham-operated mice underwent the same procedure, including treatment injections, but without ligation or puncture. Mice that died within the first 24 h post-surgery were considered to have succumbed to perioperative complications and were excluded from further analysis. Postoperative monitoring included daily weighing and 2–3 daily assessments for clinical signs of sepsis, using the Murine Sepsis Score (MSS), as described 60. Body temperature was measured at various time points using rectal thermometry. Survival was monitored every 12 h for 7 days. Humane endpoints were defined as a total MSS of 15 or the maximum score in any individual category, according to established guidelines 60.

This study applied gradient drought stress treatments to Astragalus membranaceus var. mongholicus seedlings. Treatments consisted of four levels: Control (CK), Light Drought (LD), Moderate Drought (MD), and Severe Drought (SD), corresponding to soil water contents of 80-85%, 65-70%, 50-55%, and 35-40% of saturated soil water capacity, respectively. The stress treatment was initiated at the seedling stage and lasted for 18 days. Soil moisture was precisely maintained at the predetermined levels by daily replenishment of water loss using the weighing method in the evening. Upon termination of the treatment, both aboveground (shoot) and root tissues were separately collected from plants in each treatment group. Each group contained three independent biological replicates, resulting in a total of 24 tissue samples. All samples were immediately flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen upon collection and stored at -80°C for subsequent untargeted liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) metabolomics profiling.

The preparation of polyacrylamide gels with varying stiffness was conducted as follows. Acrylamide and bis-acrylamide were dissolved in distilled water or phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) to achieve the desired final concentrations, with the specific ratios of these components determined by the target stiffness of the gel. Subsequently, ammonium persulfate (APS) and tetramethylethylenediamine (TEMED) were added to the gel solution at volumes equivalent to 1/100 and 1/1000 of the total solution volume, respectively, to initiate polymerization. The solution was then vortexed thoroughly to ensure complete mixing. The mixture was promptly transferred into a culture dish and allowed to polymerize completely. Following polymerization, any unreacted acrylamide was removed, and the gel was rinsed twice with PBS or distilled water, each rinse lasting for five minutes. To functionalize the gel surface for protein coating, approximately 500 μl of a sulfo-SANPAH solution (0.2 mg/ml)— or a volume sufficient to cover the entire gel — was applied to the gel surface. The gel was then exposed to ultraviolet light for 10 minutes at a distance of approximately 90 cm from the light source. After UV exposure, the gel was washed at least two to three times with 2 ml of 50 mM HEPES buffer to remove any excess sulfo-SANPAH. A solution containing collagen at a concentration of 0.10 mg/ml and either fibronectin or laminin at a concentration of 10 μg/ml, prepared in 50 mM HEPES, was then added to cover the gel. The gel was incubated with this protein solution overnight at 37°C. Finally, the protein-coated gel was rinsed with 2 ml of distilled water or PBS, consistent with the solvent originally used for diluting the acrylamide monomers. Primary corpus cavernosum fibroblasts were cultured on the surface of Matrigel-coated dishes with pre-adjusted stiffness. After 48 hours, the samples were collected for subsequent experiments.

After 72 hours, the medium was collected and centrifuged at 300 g for 5 minutes. White adipocyte browning was induced by exposing mature adipocytes either to tumor cell-derived secretome or extracellular vesicles (EVs) for three days. The medium was refreshed every 24 hours with new secretome or EVs. These resulting adipocytes were hereafter referred to as transdifferentiated or beige adipocytes. Cecal Ligation and Puncture (CLP)-induced high-grade sepsis. Eight-week-old male C57Bl/6J mice (Envigo, Gannat, France) were purchased and allowed to acclimate for one week. Mice were randomly assigned to treatment groups and administered either a monoclonal antibody against ACBP/DBI (α-ACBP or aDBI; 4 h and 1 h prior to surgery) or its isotype control, in combination with dexamethasone (DEX) or Phosphate-Buffered Saline (PBS) 1X, administered 1 h before CLP, as previously described 58,59. Sepsis was induced by CLP under isoflurane anesthesia. Briefly, the cecum was exteriorized, ligated at 75% of its length using non-absorbable 4-0 silk suture, and punctured once through-and-through with a 21-gauge needle. A small amount of fecal content was gently extruded, and the cecum was returned to the abdominal cavity. Sham-operated mice underwent the same procedure, including treatment injections, but without ligation or puncture. Mice that died within the first 24 h post-surgery were considered to have succumbed to perioperative complications and were excluded from further analysis. Postoperative monitoring included daily weighing and 2–3 daily assessments for clinical signs of sepsis, using the Murine Sepsis Score (MSS), as described 60. Body temperature was measured at various time points using rectal thermometry. Survival was monitored every 12 h for 7 days. Humane endpoints were defined as a total MSS of 15 or the maximum score in any individual category, according to established guidelines 60.

Twenty specific pathogen-free (SPF) female C57 BL/6 J mice (8 weeks old, body weight 16–20 g) that had never been pregnant, and 5 SPF male C57 BL/6 J mice (8 weeks old, body weight 20–25 g) were selected. After 1 week of acclimatization in the laboratory animal center, the intervention was initiated. The female mice were randomly divided into 2 groups (10 mice per group): ① Control group; ② TCS exposure group (50 mg/kg/day TCS), hereinafter referred to as the MTCS group. Male mice were housed under normal conditions and used solely for mating. Pregnant mice were housed individually when pregnancy was confirmed around embryonic day 18 (E18). TCS (97%, Sigma-Aldrich, USA) was dissolved in corn oil (Aladdin, China) as a vehicle and stored at room temperature. Using the no-observed-adverse-effect level (NOAEL) of TCS (50 mg/kg/day) as the moderate exposure dose, two dose groups (0 mg/kg/day for the control group, 50 mg/kg/day for the moderate exposure group) were set up to establish a mouse TCS exposure model. Adult pregnant female mice were exposed via gavage at a volume of 1 mL per 100 g body weight. Before each gavage, the body weight was measured to calculate the exposure volume, and gavage was performed once daily. The day on which a vaginal plug was detected was defined as E 0 (Embryonic Day), and gavage was administered continuously from E4 to E21. The first day of parturition was defined as PND 0 (Postnatal Day), and gavage was continued from PND3 to PND21, resulting in a total exposure duration of 35 days.

Given that a total cumulative dose of 8 mg/kg is the safest threshold without significant potential for cardiotoxicity in rats, we opted for dosing DOX as 2mg/kg once a week, for 4 weeks. This has also been used to establish CMB elsewhere. TMZ was given as 25 mg/kg, based on a previous study. TMZ, at doses between 75 and 200 mg/m² (approximately 2–5 mg/kg), has been effectively used in humans for over ten years to treat brain tumours. TMZ was administered once daily for three consecutive days, followed by a four-day recovery period, over a span of four weeks. This cyclic treatment was chosen because it mirrors the most commonly employed protocol in humans, which involves giving 200 mg/m² per day for five consecutive days every four weeks. For the combination regimen, the agents were administered once weekly to minimize overlapping toxicities while preserving potential synergistic interactions. 65 subjects with obesity from the same geographical region were included in this study. Subjects were recruited through printed advertisement. All subjects were screened for medical history and underwent physical examinations prior to enrollment. All subjects provided informed written consent. This study has been approved by the Ethics Committee of the Medical University of Vienna (no. 1032/2013 and no. 1071/2017) and was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT02381483 and NCT03168009). The study was conducted at the Division of Endocrinology and Metabolism, Department of Medicine III and at the Department for Biomedical Imaging and Image-guided Therapy, Division of Nuclear Medicine, Medical University of Vienna in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. Study participants were examined in the morning after an overnight fast (>8h). After a blood draw and a resting phase of 30 minutes an indirect calorimetry was performed in order to determine the resting energy expenditure (REE) using a computerized open circuit indirect calorimeter (Quark RMR, Cosmed, Rome, Italy). Afterwards the subjects were fitted with a water-perfused cooling vest (CoolShirt Systems, Stockbridge, Georgia, USA) and the water temperature was kept slightly above the shivering temperature as determined by surface electromyography (OT Bioelettronica, Torino, Italy). Cold exposure was applied for 150 minutes followed by a second indirect calorimetry after 60 minutes in order to determine the cold induced thermogenesis (CIT). After 90 min of cold exposure 18F-FDG was administered, and cold exposure was continued for another 60 min until the PET/CT acquisition started. Subjects that had 18F-FDG positive BAT depots after cold exposure were deemed as BAT positive, whereas subjects that had no significant 18F-FDG uptake after cold exposure were considered BAT negative. All 18F-PET/CT scans were performed during the cool season (fall to spring) to avoid any seasonal influence on BAT activity.

32 healthy 3-month-old zebrafish were randomly allocated into four groups (n=8 per group), including one blank control group and three drug-treated groups. All procedures were approved by Duke University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee and performed according to the regulations of the committee. Young male and female Wistar rats were purchased from Envigo (http://www.envigo.com), and arrived at 3 weeks of age to be acclimated to our vivarium for one week, during which time they were feed ad-libitum on standard chow (SC) diet (LabDiet, Rodent diet 5053, https://www.labdiet.com), and housed with a reversed light cycle (9 AM OFF/9 PM ON). At 4 weeks of age, rats were subjected to one of two food insecurity protocols, the first involving feeding of standard chow (SC) diet and the second involving feeding of high fat/high sucrose (HF/HS) diet (Research Diets, D12451i). Both the SC- and HF/HS diet-fed rats were divided into 2 groups of female and 2 groups of male rats, with 6 rats/group. In the first protocol, one group from each sex was fed SC diet ad-libitum (ad lib, AL group) and a second group was also fed SC diet, but subjected to food insecurity (FI), each for a period of 20 days. In the second protocol, one group from each sex was fed HF/HS diet ad-libitum (AL) and a second group was also fed HF/HS diet, but subjected to food insecurity (FI), each for a period of 20 days. For both protocols, the FI intervention involved provision of less food, and in a sporadic pattern compared to the AL group. Following the 20-day intervention period, both the FI and AL groups were allowed to feed ad-libitum, either on SC diet in protocol 1, or on HF/HS diet in protocol 2, for an additional period of 55 days. Blood samples were taken prior to the onset of the FI intervention period, immediately following the FI intervention period, and at 1, 3 and 5 weeks after the FI intervention. Approximately 150-200 µl of blood was collected via the saphenous vein, and plasma stored at -80oC for further analyses. Fifty days after the start of the experiment, and 30 days after the end of the FI intervention period, we measured body composition by TD-NMR, using a Bruker minispec LF90 (https://www.bruker.com). At day 75 of the protocol, or 55 days after the end of the FI intervention, we began a sequence in which 8 rats at a time, comprised of 2 female FI, 2 female AL, 2 male FI and 2 male AL rats were moved to Promethion Core ® (https://www.sablesys.com) metabolic cages, in which they were allowed to equilibrate for 3 days prior to 4 consecutive days of noninvasive analysis of energy expenditure and physical activity, with ad-lib feeding on the diet consumed in their respective protocols (SC or HF/HS). Data analyses were performed using an on-line application CalR (https://calrapp.org). Following this sequence, animals were returned to their original cages for an additional 2 weeks of feeding prior to sacrifice.

Exosomes were isolated from ~275 µL of plasma using polymer-based precipitation followed by immune-affinity purification. Samples were cleared (12,000 x g, 15 min), supernatants were mixed with protease/phosphatase inhibitor cocktail(PI/PhI, Thermo Scientific, 87786), and incubated in ExoQuick (System Biosciences LLC; EQULTRA-20A-1; 60 min, 4°C), pelleted (3,000 x g, 10 min), resuspended in 1:1 Buffers A/B, passed through spin columns, and stored at -80°C or processed immediately. For enrichment, eluates were incubated with biotinylated antibodies against GLAST (astrocytic) (Miltenyi Biotec, Cat. 130-118-984) in 3% BSA/DPBS (4°C), followed by streptavidin agarose bead capture (Thermo Scientific, 53114; 4°C). Bead bound exosomes were washed and eluted with 0.1 M glycine-HCl (pH 3), neutralized with Tris-HCl (pH 8), left unlysed, resuspended in 125 uL particle-free water, and frozen at -80°C. Primary human astrocytes grown in 6-well plates were treated with astrocyte-derived exosome samples or positive/negative controls and incubated for 24-hours. Under controlled conditions: we captured 16 adult P. nathusii (8 male, 8 female, body mass = 8.7 ± 1.2 g; mean ± standard deviation) at the Pape Bird Ringing Station, Latvia (56°09′57′′ N 21°01′02′′ E, Rucava municipality), during the migration season in September 2020 under permit number 184/2020 of the Latvian Nature Conservation Agency. After five days of acclimatization, bats were transferred to Lund University, where they were kept in indoor cages in groups of four under the permit number 5.8.18-1012472018 of the Lund-Malmö board for ethics in animal research. Whilst in captivity bats were hand fed a diet of Tenebrio molitor larvae (mealworms) supplemented with juvenile hand-feeding formula (Harrison’s Bird Foods, Tennessee USA), and were provided water ad libitum in cages. In Lund, bats were trained to fly in a low-turbulence wind tunnel in pairs at wind speeds between 6 and 8 m s-1 (Pennycuick et al. 1997), which is close to the flight speeds of migratory bats in the field (Troxell et al., 2019). An individual was considered trained when it flew for more than 10 minutes without landing, which took between three and seven training days. Following this training, we began experimental flights with individuals flying in pairs for at least 30 minutes. All flight training and experimental flights took place during the active phase of the bats between sunset and 2 am. Bats were fasted for at least 16 hours prior to flight and were fed and given water after each experimental flight. In nature Nathusius’s pipistrelles occasionally forage until dawn and will not become active again until ~1 hour after sunset, therefore inactive (or fasting periods) are at least 11 to 18 hours per day in their summer/autumn range. Each individual underwent two experimental flights, which were conducted on separate days and in a randomized order to ensure that blood volume was replenished between flights. Whole blood samples were collected immediately after flight (post-exercise) or one hour after the flight (recovery). At the end of the entire experimental period, after one week of no flight experiments, a third blood sample was taken during the rest phase between 10 am and 2 pm from each individual in a fasted state (resting). Under field conditions: we collected blood samples from free-ranging bats prior to and during the migration season in Latvia under permit number 114 issued by the Food and Veterinary Service to the Faculty of Veterinary Medicine of the Latvia University of Agriculture and permit number 184/2020 of the Latvian Nature Conservation Agency. All bats were captured in mid-flight using mist nets or a hand net. Similar to the controlled wind tunnel experiments, whole blood was collected either immediately post-exercise (within 3 minutes of capture in flight), or after one hour of recovery.

Five queenright double brood chamber colonies were split into 20 nucleus colonies on May 27, 2022, at an apiary located at the University of Lethbridge, with each parent colony split into four small nucleus colonies (nucs). Each of the four nucs from each parent colony was randomly assigned to one of four treatments: queenright and broodright (QRBR), queenless and broodright (QLBR), queenright and broodless (QRBL), or queenless and broodless (QLBL). A queen excluder was placed between the two brood chambers prior to splitting the parent colonies to isolate the queen and reduce the number of eggs and open brood in one of the brood chambers to facilitate setting up the broodless treatment colonies. All parent queens were removed from their colonies upon splitting and mated queens imported from California were introduced to the experimental colonies in the two queenright treatments on May 27, 2022. All experimental colonies received frames containing equal amounts of pollen, nectar, and bees from their parent colonies. Broodright nucs (i.e., QRBR and QLBR treatments) were supplied with frames containing brood of all stages (egg, larvae, and pupae) from parent colonies at the time of initial set up. Frames containing open brood from unrelated non-experimental colonies were added every four days to the QLBR experimental colonies to ensure the presence of open brood throughout the experiment. To mimic the swapping of one frame experienced by all QLBR colonies and equalize levels of disturbance across all experimental colonies, all other experimental colonies underwent “sham moves”, where a single frame was removed from and replaced within each experimental colony. Broodless experimental colonies (e.g., QRBL and QLBL) received frames that did not contain open brood or had open brood removed and instead received additional frames of pollen and nectar. Queens in the QRBL experimental colonies were confined to a large cage made from queen excluder material that enabled their interaction with workers but inhibited their access to comb to lay eggs. Queen and brood status were monitored every four days for the presence/absence of a queen and open brood. On June 15, 2022, approximately 100 bees were sampled from the center frame of each experimental colony using 50 mL falcon tubes. Tubes were placed on dry ice until storage in a -80°C freezer.

we used a comprehensive analytical pipeline for integrating metabolomics and metagenomics data to elucidate host-microbe metabolic interactions. The process begins with raw mass spectrometry data (KK-US⁻, KK⁺US⁻, KK⁺US⁺) that undergoes preprocessing through xMSanalyzer, including format conversion, noise filtering, peak matching and extraction, followed by quality control via PCA and total ion current normalization. Statistical analysis is then performed using Polyomics integrated Metabolomics Pipeline (PiMP), employing both PCA and PLS-DA to identify differential metabolites based on stringent criteria (fold change ≥1.2 or <0.83, VIP≥1.5, and P-value < 0.05). The identified differential metabolites are subsequently analyzed using the AMON tool, which integrates three key data sources: KEGG orthology identifiers from identified Schistosoma mansoni metagenome biomarkers (bacteria), KEGG orthology identifiers from the Homo sapiens metabolome (host), and KEGG compound IDs of the differential metabolites obtained from LC/MS Untargeted metabolomics.

The experimental design comprised a three-factor pot study evaluating the interactive effects of continuous cropping history, drought intensity, and drought duration on cassava. Prior to planting, soil that had undergone two consecutive cycles of cassava cultivation (designated as the 2‑cycle continuous cropping soil) and soil that had been maintained under fallow conditions without cassava planting for the same period (designated as the 0‑cycle control soil) were collected. Both soil types were thoroughly homogenized separately and then filled into planting boxes (internal dimensions: 36 cm length × 36 cm width × 46 cm height), with each box containing 60 kg of the respective soil. The study incorporated the following three experimental factors and their specific levels: Cropping condition (Continuous cropping history): Two levels — 0 cycles (non-continuous cropping control) and 2 cycles (continuous cropping). Drought intensity: Two levels — Well-watered (WA, 75 ± 5% of field capacity) and Severe drought (SD, 25 ± 5% of field capacity). Drought duration: Two levels — 0 days (non-stress sampling baseline) and 14 days (sustained stress). Drought stress imposition was initiated at 60 days after planting. The 0‑day drought duration samples were collected immediately prior to the onset of differential watering regimes at this 60‑day time point, thereby serving as the pre‑stress baseline. For the 14‑day drought duration treatment, plants were subjected to the assigned watering regimes continuously for 14 days following stress initiation, with samples harvested at the conclusion of this period. The combination of these factors resulted in a total of six distinct treatment groups: (1) 0‑cycle soil + Well-watered + 0 days; (2) 0‑cycle soil + Well-watered + 14 days; (3) 0‑cycle soil + Severe drought + 14 days; (4) 2‑cycle soil + Well-watered + 0 days; (5) 2‑cycle soil + Well-watered + 14 days; (6) 2‑cycle soil + Severe drought + 14 days. Notably, since the 0‑day samples were collected at the moment of stress initiation (60 days after planting), the drought intensity factor does not apply to this time point in terms of physiological effect, although all pots were maintained under well-watered conditions until drought treatments commenced. Each of the six treatments was replicated across six individual pots (n = 6). Two cassava stem cuttings of the elite cultivar SC205 were planted per pot, and after emergence, seedlings were thinned to retain one uniform plant per cutting, resulting in two plants per pot. Soil moisture levels were monitored daily using a portable soil moisture meter, and water was adjusted accordingly to maintain the target field capacity thresholds throughout the experimental period.

Forty 6-week-old C57BL/6 mouse mice were randomly divided into four groups: a control group (Control), a dextran sulfate sodium-induced colitis group (DSS), a DSS plus *Lactococcus lactis* subsp. *lactis* sef432 treatment group (DSS-LA), and a DSS plus mesalazine treatment group (DSS-5-ASA, used as a positive control). From day 1 to day 7, except for the Control group, mice in all other groups were provided with drinking water containing 3% dextran sulfate sodium (DSS) to induce Ulcerative colitis. From day 8 to day 14, mice in the DSS-LA group were orally gavaged daily with 1 × 10⁹ CFU of *L. lactis* subsp. *lactis* sef432. Mice in the Control and DSS groups received an equal volume of sterile MRS medium by gavage, while mice in the DSS-5-ASA group were administered 100 mg/kg of Mesalazine daily. During the experiment, body weight, general health status (including coat condition, constipation, hematochezia, and mental status), and mortality were monitored and recorded. The disease activity index (DAI) was calculated based on body weight loss, stool consistency, and fecal bleeding to evaluate the severity of colitis. On day 15, all mice were euthanized by cervical dislocation. Cecal contents were collected and stored at −80°C. The colon was excised, and its length and weight were measured, after which it was divided into two parts: the proximal colon was stored at −80°C, and the distal colon was fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde solution.

A factorial experimental matrix was established to evaluate the combined effects of nitrogen availability and carbon enrichment. Pre-renal azotemia was induced as previously described. Briefly, baseline kidney function was measured via transcutaneous glomerular filtration rate (tGFR) in mice 24 hours prior to time 0. At time 0, food and water were withheld and then mice were randomized to receive either intraperitoneal (IP) injections of either 150 µL normal saline (NS) (Veh group) or 4 mg furosemide (Sigma Aldrich, St. Louis, Missouri, USA) dissolved in 150 µL NS (40 mg/mL) (PRA group) at times 0 and 3 hours. At 6 hours, tGFR was measured to confirm unchanged (Veh) or decreased (PRA) GFR. Mice were euthanized and whole blood samples obtained (6 hr Veh and 6 hr PRA). A separate cohort of Veh and PRA mice had tGFR measured at 6 hours and then received 1 mL NS IP at times 7, 8, and 23 hours and had ad libitum access to food and water up to time 24 hours at which time tGFR was measured to confirm kidney function had been restored to baseline. Mice were then euthanized and whole blood samples obtained (24 hr Veh and 24 hr PRA with restoration of kidney function [24 hrPRA-R]). Blood urea nitrogen (BUN) was also measured to assess PRA resolution in 24 hr PRA-R group. Unmanipulated mice (Normal) were used as an additional control. Normal mice had full access to food and water and did not receive vehicle injections (this cohort was separate from the Normal cohort used in the ischemic AKI experimental group – see next section). Thus, the PRA experimental cohort included 5 different groups: Normal, 6 hr Veh, 6 hr PRA, 24 hr Veh, and 24 hr PRA-R. 10 mice were used in each experimental group; however, tGFR data for one mouse in the 24 hr PRA-R group was accidentally deleted and the confirmatory BUN testing did not suggest resolution of PRA and thus was excluded from the 24 hr PRA-R group leaving 9 mice in this group.

Preparation of maturation medium (MM11) MM11 supplement contains 11 factors (fatty acids, hormones, 2-phospho-L-ascorbic acid trisodium salt, retinoic acid, L-carnitine, and transferrin. The basal medium is DMEM without glucose (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and 2% NeuroBasal (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Before maturation, human iPSC-CMs were maintained in RPMI-B27. Maturation treatment was initiated on or after day 20 of differentiation and consisted of three sequential stages. In the first stage, iPSC-CMs at 50–85% confluency were gradually transitioned to a DMEM-based culture by feeding them with a 1:1 mixture of RPMI-B27 and low-glucose DMEM with B27 (DMEM-B27) for two days, followed by one day in 100% DMEM-B27. This transition allowed the cells to adapt to the DMEM formulation, which more closely reflects physiological calcium concentrations. In the second stage, cells were cultured in MM11 medium for 10 days, with medium change every other day. In the final stage, cells were switched to a recovery medium consisting of low-glucose DMEM supplemented with B27 minus insulin, 80 μM BSA-palmitic acid, 30 μM BSA-oleic acid, and 10 nM insulin. After 2–3 days in the recovery medium, the mature iPSC-CMs were subjected to functional and molecular assays. To further characterize the metabolic phenotype of MM11-treated cells, global metabolomic profiling was conducted, alongside iPSC-CMs generated using a previously published maturation protocol as described by the authors (Feyen et al. Cell Reports 2020, PMID:32697997) and age-matched Controls.

To induce neural differentiation, iPSCs at 70-80% confluency were directed toward neural progenitor cells (NPCs) following an established protocol (DOI: 10.1152/jn.00045.2024). In brief, 0.5 x106 iPSCs were seeded in Essential 8 medium supplemented with 10 μM Revita on a 6-well plate and incubated overnight. The following day, cells were fed with Neural Induction Medium (Neurobasal medium + 1% Neural Induction Supplement, Life Technologies) and incubated for 7 days with regular medium change every other day. On the eighth day, the medium was replaced with Neural Expansion Medium (0.5X Neurobasal medium, 0.5X KnockOut™ DMEM/F12, 1X Neural Induction Supplement) and maintained for 48 hours promote NPC commitment. On day 10, 1x10e6 NPCs were passaged onto poly-D-lysine/Rh-laminin-coated plate and fed with Neural Expansion Medium containing 10 μM Revita and incubated for 24 hours. On the following day, the media was replaced with Neural Differentiation medium (0.5X Neurobasal medium, 0.5X DMEM/F12, 0.5X N2 supplement, 125 mM GlutaMAX, 10 ng/ml bFGF and 1X B27 supplement). Medium was changed on alternate days over the course of one month, after which neurons were harvested as described above for mass spectrometry processing.

We have utilized a genetic mouse model (Plp1-iCKO-Myrf) during postnatal myelination, demyelination, and remyelination for our study. For the postnatal myelination, mouse brain and spinal cord tissues were collected at the postnatal timepoints of P1, P4, P7, P10, P14, P21, and P42. These Plp1-iCKO-Myrf postnatal mice were not treated with tamoxifen and are referred to as N/A for the treatment and genotype in the data table. The next set of Plp1-iCKO-Myrf mice at 8 weeks of age were administered intraperitoneal injections of tamoxifen for five days at 8 weeks of age (100 µL of 20 mg/mL daily in corn oil) to induce Myrf ablation and demyelination. The mouse progeny can be either Cre positive (presence of CreERT gene) or negative (absence of CreERT gene). After tamoxifen injection, Cre-positive mice lose Myrf in oligodendrocytes and undergo demyelination (myelin loss). These Cre-positive mice go through a peak demyelination by week 12 post-tamoxifen, and then undergo remyelination (myelin repair) from 18-30 weeks post-tamoxifen. There are no major effects of tamoxifen on myelin in the Cre-negative mice, and they serve as the healthy controls for the study. In summary, Cre-positive refers to demyelinated mice, and Cre-negative are the healthy/control mice. We have collected brain and spinal cord tissues at week 6, week 12, week 18, week 24, and week 30. In addition, a randomly chosen subset of mice at week 12 and week 18 post tamoxifen injection received Sob-AM2 chow treatment starting 2 weeks post-tamoxifen. Sob-AM2 was compounded into chow (Envigo Teklad 2016 diet) at a dose of 420 µg/ kg chow (a nominal daily dose of 84 µg/ kg body weight). These mice were used to test the Sob-AM2 drug effect with demyelination.

HPLM was prepared as previously described (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2017.03.023). Tracer-containing HPLM library was prepared and nitrogen metabolism profiling experiments performed as previously described (https://doi.org/10.1038/s42255-026-01520-0) with the addition of a medium containing 15N3-creatine (Cambridge Isotope Laboratories NLM-9218). Tracer-containing HPLM used in nitrogen metabolism profiling was generated identically to the unlabeled version, with labeled metabolites replacing their unlabeled counterparts at equimolar concentrations. Tracer HPLM was assembled by mixing thawed frozen or freshly-prepared stocks of unlabeled HPLM pools, replacing one pool per tracing condition with a version containing an individual 15N tracer. Media was adjusted to pH 7.4 using NaOH or HCl, then diluted to the final volume with ultrapure water, sterile filtered with a 0.22 μm PES filter (Millipore Sigma SCGP00525, Corning 431153, Corning 431097, or Corning 431098), and supplemented as described below. HPLM was prepared without glutamate, except for conditions in which glutamate was traced. For culture of TS516 glioma stem-like cells, HPLM was supplemented with 1 × B27 supplement (Thermo Fisher 17504044); 0.25 × N2 supplement (Thermo Fisher 17502048); 20 ng/mL EGF (GoldBio 1150-04); 20 ng/mL bFGF (GoldBio 1140-02); 2 μg/mL heparin (STEMCELL Technologies 07980); 50 U/mL and 50 μg/mL, respectively, penicillin/streptomycin (Thermo Fisher 15-140-148); 125 ng/mL amphotericin B (GeminiBio 400104); and 0.25 μg/mL Plasmocin (InvivoGen ant-mpp). For culture of differentiated NHA Donor #1 cells, HPLM was supplemented with 10% dialyzed FBS (GeminiBio 100-108) and 100 U/mL and 100 μg/mL, respectively, of penicillin/streptomycin (Thermo Fisher 15140148). NHA Donor #1 cells were plated in 6-well plates (2.5 × 10^4 cells per well) in 2 mL DMEM prepared as described above. TS516 cells were plated in 6-well ultra-low adherence plates (2 × 10^5 cells per well) in 2 mL NeuroCult NS-A Basal Medium (Human) prepared as described above. After 24 hours, 2 mL unlabeled HPLM prepared as described above was added to produce a mixture of 50% native medium and 50% HPLM. 24 hours later, media was changed to 100% unlabeled HPLM (10 mL for NHA Donor #1 cells and 4.5 mL for TS516 cells). 24 hours later, media was changed to fresh 100% HPLM with one nitrogen-containing metabolite per sample exchanged for an equimolar amount of its 15N-labeled counterpart (10 mL for NHA Donor #1 cells, 4.5 mL for TS516 cells). After 18 hours, samples were harvested, washed with ice-cold normal saline, snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and subsequently prepared for LC-MS analysis as described below.

Animals were transferred immediately after surgery to a clean room and cage containing sterile bedding chips and placed on a heating pad to prevent hypothermia. Animals were checked on 2 hours post-surgery and twice more within a 24-hour period. Animals had unrestricted access to food and water within their cage.

Spermatogenesis was synchronized as previously described (Biol Reprod, DOI: 10.1095/biolreprod.113.109843). Briefly, 2-day-old mice received daily oral dosing of WIN 18,446 (100 μg/g body weight) suspended in 1% gum tragacanth for 7 consecutive days. After the final treatment, testes were collected and digested with type I collagenase followed by 0.25% trypsin to obtain single-cell suspensions (Biol Reprod, DOI: 10.1095/biolreprod.115.136507). The resulting cell suspension was centrifuged and resuspended in PBS containing 2% bovine serum albumin (BSA) at 1 × 10⁶ cells/100 μL. After incubation with APC-conjugated anti-c-Kit antibody for 30 min at 4℃, Oct4-GFP+/c-Kit- SSC were isolated by flow cytometry. Twenty-four hours after the final WIN 18,446 dose, mice received an intraperitoneal injection of retinoic acid (RA; 25 μg/g body weight in DMSO) to initiate synchronized spermatogonial differentiation. At 130 h post-RA injection, testes were collected and processed as aforementioned, and differentiating spermatogonia (c-Kit+) were isolated by flow cytometry. For the collection of spermatocytes and spermatids at defined stages, testes were digested and stained with Hoechst 33342, and 1N and 4N cell populations were sorted by flow cytometry. Spermatocytes and spermatids were collected at 168 h (preL), 312 h (P), 432 h (RS2), and 540 h (RS8) post-RA injection. SSC refers to Spermatogonial Stem Cells (Oct4-GFP+/c-Kit-), Diff.ing SPG refers to Differentiating Spermatogonia (c-Kit+).
